questions.question: What are all things made of?
questions.explanation: Atoms are the building blocks of ordinary matter.

questions.question: What is the name of the chart that organises the chemical elements?
questions.explanation: Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version in 1869.

questions.question: What are the cells of the nervous system called?
questions.explanation: Neurons carry signals as electrical impulses.

questions.question: Roughly how many hours of sleep do most adults need each night?
questions.explanation: Most adults function best with seven to nine hours.

questions.question: What is the name of the chemical messengers carried in the blood?
questions.explanation: Hormones are released by glands.

questions.question: What is the basic unit of life?
questions.explanation: All living things are made of one or more cells.

questions.question: Which instrument do we use to see very small things such as cells?
questions.explanation: Microscopes magnify tiny objects.

questions.question: How do your cells make more cells when you grow or heal a cut?
questions.explanation: A cell splits into two new cells.

questions.question: At sea-level pressure, at what temperature does pure water boil?
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at standard sea-level pressure.

questions.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?
questions.explanation: Diamond ranks 10 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness.

questions.question: Earth's air is made up mostly of which gas?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78 percent, oxygen about 21.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
choices: Gases in the air trap some of the Sun's heat
questions.explanation: Without it Earth would be far colder.

questions.question: What are clouds made of?
choices: Tiny water droplets or ice crystals
questions.explanation: Water vapour condenses on particles in the air.

questions.question: What are the two digits used in binary code?
questions.explanation: Computers store data as bits.

questions.question: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN?
questions.explanation: Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989 and built the first website in 1990 to 1991.

questions.question: What does AI stand for?
questions.explanation: AI means machines doing tasks that normally require human intelligence.

questions.question: Which galaxy do we live in?
questions.explanation: The Solar System sits in one of its spiral arms.

questions.question: What is the name of the theory that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense state?
questions.explanation: The universe has expanded and cooled since.

questions.question: What is the boundary around a black hole called, beyond which light cannot escape?
questions.explanation: Nothing can return from inside it.

questions.question: What do we call a complete path that electric current can flow around?
questions.explanation: The path must be unbroken for current to flow.

questions.question: What makes your hair stand up when you rub a balloon on it?
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons, leaving opposite charges that attract.

questions.question: What are the two ends of a magnet called?
questions.explanation: Opposite poles attract.

questions.question: A moving object has which kind of energy?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed.

questions.question: Which of these is a good conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals conduct heat well.

questions.question: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Wind and sunlight are replenished naturally.

questions.question: Which scientist is famous for the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.explanation: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

questions.question: What are the preserved remains of ancient living things called?
questions.explanation: Fossils are typically found in sedimentary rock.

questions.question: In a food chain, what do we call organisms such as grass that make their own food?
questions.explanation: Producers capture energy from sunlight.

questions.question: The fear of spiders has what name?
questions.explanation: Arachne is the Greek word for spider.

questions.question: Which almond-shaped part of the brain is central to the fear response?
questions.explanation: The amygdala helps detect threats.

questions.question: Which Russian scientist trained dogs to salivate at the sound of a bell?
questions.explanation: His conditioning experiments began around 1900.

questions.question: Which brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903?
questions.explanation: Orville and Wilbur flew at Kitty Hawk.

questions.question: Which was the first artificial satellite launched into orbit, in 1957?
questions.explanation: The Soviet Union launched it on 4 October 1957.

questions.question: Which NASA rover landed in Gale Crater on Mars in 2012?
questions.explanation: Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in August 2012.

questions.question: What do we call a picture that tricks the brain into seeing something that is not really there?
questions.explanation: Illusions show that perception is built by the brain, not just received.

questions.question: Which part of memory holds a phone number for a few seconds?
questions.explanation: Working memory holds about seven items briefly.

questions.question: In a medical trial, what is a placebo?
choices: A treatment with no active ingredient
questions.explanation: Placebos help separate real effects from expectation.

questions.question: Which simple machine is a seesaw?
questions.explanation: A seesaw balances around a pivot.

questions.question: Why is a sharp knife better at cutting than a blunt one?
choices: Force is concentrated on a smaller area
questions.explanation: Pressure equals force divided by area.

questions.question: What must be burned for a petrol car engine to run?
questions.explanation: Fuel burns and the expanding gases push the pistons.

questions.question: What is steel mainly made of?
questions.explanation: Carbon makes iron much stronger.

questions.question: Which element is the main material in most computer chips?
questions.explanation: Silicon is a semiconductor.

questions.question: Which metal is key to most rechargeable phone batteries?
questions.explanation: Lithium-ion batteries are light and energy dense.

questions.question: What is 2 + 3 × 4?
questions.explanation: Multiplication is done before addition: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.

questions.question: Rounded to the nearest ten, what is 347?
questions.explanation: The units digit 7 is 5 or more, so 347 rounds up to 350.

questions.question: How many degrees do the interior angles of a triangle add up to?
questions.explanation: The three interior angles of any flat triangle sum to 180 degrees.

questions.question: The diameter of a circle is how many times its radius?
questions.explanation: The diameter passes through the centre and is twice the radius.

questions.question: If x + 7 = 12, what is x?
questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: x = 12 − 7 = 5.

questions.question: What is 2⁵?
What is the mean of 2, 4 and 9?
questions.explanation: The sum is 15 and there are three numbers, so the mean is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

questions.question: Which of these is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 13 has no divisors except 1 and itself. 15, 21 and 27 are all multiples of 3.

questions.question: What is the name of the theorem a² + b² = c² for right-angled triangles?
questions.explanation: The Pythagorean theorem links the two shorter sides a and b to the hypotenuse c.

questions.question: How many metres are in a kilometre?
questions.explanation: Kilo means one thousand.

questions.question: What comes next in the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16, …?
questions.explanation: Each term is double the one before, so the next is 32.

questions.question: What is a hypothesis?
questions.explanation: Scientists test hypotheses with experiments.

questions.question: Which unit measures length in the metric system?
questions.explanation: The metre is the SI unit of length.

questions.question: Who developed the theory of relativity?
questions.explanation: Einstein published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1915.

questions.question: What force pulls objects toward the Earth?
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls masses toward each other.

questions.question: Who is famous for describing the laws of motion and gravity?
questions.explanation: Newton published the Principia in 1687.

questions.question: If a car travels 100 km in 2 hours, what is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed equals distance divided by time.

questions.question: Who discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium and won two Nobel Prizes?
questions.explanation: She won in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.

questions.question: Which element is the main fuel in most nuclear power stations?
questions.explanation: Uranium-235 undergoes fission.

questions.question: What kind of nuclear reaction powers the stars?
questions.explanation: Nuclei join and release energy.

questions.question: Which ocean is the biggest on Earth by area?
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of the planet.

questions.question: What is a powerful river-like flow of seawater called?
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream is a famous example.

questions.question: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called what?
questions.explanation: Polyps secrete hard calcium carbonate skeletons.

questions.question: Arachnophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Arachnophobia is an intense fear of spiders and other arachnids.

questions.question: Claustrophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Claustrophobia is the fear of enclosed or confined spaces, such as lifts or tunnels.

questions.question: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Light travels at about 299,792 km/s in a vacuum, usually rounded to 300,000 km/s.

questions.question: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravity continually pulls the planets toward it, bending their paths into orbits.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle carries a negative electric charge?
questions.explanation: Electrons carry negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons are neutral.

questions.question: What kind of energy does a moving object have?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, equal to ½mv².

questions.question: Why are some old window panes thicker at the bottom?
choices: The way they were made left them uneven
They were always fitted upside down by mistake
Glass slowly flows downward over centuries
questions.explanation: Old crown glass was uneven and glaziers often put the thicker edge down; glass does not flow at room temperature on human timescales.
questions.misconception: Many people think old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward.

questions.question: What do plants make using sunlight?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What do the roots of a plant do?
choices: Take in water and anchor the plant
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and minerals and hold the plant in the ground.

questions.question: Which part of a flowering plant becomes the fruit?
questions.explanation: After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit around the seeds.

questions.question: What gas must be present for a fire to burn in air?
questions.explanation: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen.

questions.question: Lemon juice tastes sour because it is what?
questions.explanation: Citric acid gives lemons their sourness.

questions.question: What is the orange-brown crust that forms on iron left in damp air?
questions.explanation: Rust is iron oxide.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms from cooled lava?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form from molten rock.

questions.question: What are the large slabs of the Earth's crust called?
questions.explanation: They move a few centimetres per year.

questions.question: What is the hot, dense centre of the Earth called?
questions.explanation: The core is mostly iron and nickel.

questions.question: Which organ lets us see?
questions.explanation: Light enters the eye and is sensed at the back.

questions.question: Which part of the body do we use to hear?
questions.explanation: Sound waves enter the ear canal and reach the eardrum.

questions.question: Which sense do you use mostly to detect odours?
questions.explanation: Receptors in the nose detect airborne chemicals.

questions.question: Which planet orbits nearest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury orbits the Sun in just 88 days.

questions.question: What does the Moon orbit?
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits Earth about once every 27 days.

questions.question: What causes day and night on Earth?
questions.explanation: Earth turns once about every 24 hours.

questions.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide (rust) on its surface gives Mars its reddish colour.

questions.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.explanation: There are eight: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is about 150 million km away; the next nearest, Proxima Centauri, is over 4 light-years away.

questions.question: What is true about the far side of the Moon?
choices: It receives as much sunlight as the near side over a month
It is always in Earth's shadow
questions.explanation: The Moon turns once per orbit, so every part of it has day and night. We just never see that side from Earth.
questions.misconception: Many people think the far side of the Moon is permanently dark.

questions.question: What is the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun is an average star.

questions.question: What is faster: sound or light?
questions.explanation: Light travels almost a million times faster than sound in air.

questions.question: Where are new stars born?
choices: In clouds of gas and dust
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls clouds of gas called nebulae together.

questions.question: Which of these is a solid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Iron is a solid; mercury is a liquid and oxygen and steam are gases.

questions.question: What do we call water in its solid form?
questions.explanation: Water freezes to ice at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.question: What happens when you stir sugar into hot water?
questions.explanation: The sugar spreads out as molecules among the water, forming a solution.

questions.question: What do sound waves need to travel?
questions.explanation: Sound cannot travel in empty space.

questions.question: What colours does a rainbow show?
questions.explanation: Water droplets split sunlight into its colours.

questions.question: Which type of wave carries your radio station?
questions.explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves.

questions.question: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called what?
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon but have different neutron counts.

questions.question: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78% of the atmosphere; oxygen is about 21%.

questions.question: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7.

questions.question: Whose X-ray images helped Watson and Crick work out the structure of DNA in 1953?
questions.explanation: Franklin's Photo 51 revealed the helical shape.

questions.question: Which monk discovered the basic laws of inheritance by breeding pea plants?
questions.explanation: Mendel's experiments were in the 1850s and 1860s.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.explanation: We have 23 pairs: one set from each parent.

questions.question: Which scientist discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.explanation: Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould, Penicillium, killed bacteria on a culture plate.

questions.question: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm?
questions.explanation: Area = half × base × height = 0.5 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².

questions.question: What is (−3) × (−4)?
questions.explanation: A negative multiplied by a negative gives a positive: 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.question: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. What is the probability that the next flip is heads?
questions.explanation: Flips are independent, so the coin has no memory. The next flip is still 1/2.

questions.question: A whole number is divisible by 9 exactly when what is true?
choices: It is odd and divisible by 3
Its digits add up to a multiple of 9
Its last two digits are divisible by 9
questions.explanation: The digit-sum rule works for 9: for example 729 has digits summing to 18, so it is divisible by 9.

questions.question: Oxygen is necessary for a fire. What does this mean?
choices: Oxygen alone is enough to start a fire
Without oxygen there can be no fire
questions.explanation: A necessary condition must be present, but it does not guarantee the result by itself.

questions.question: Which mathematician proved the Poincaré conjecture, in work published in 2002 and 2003?
questions.explanation: Perelman posted his proof online and later declined the Fields Medal and the Clay prize.

questions.question: Roughly how many seconds are there in one day?
In how many different orders can three people stand in a queue?
questions.explanation: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 arrangements.

questions.question: Which famous constant is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter?
questions.explanation: Pi is approximately 3.14159 and its decimals never end or repeat.

questions.question: In a room of 23 people, the chance that at least two share a birthday is closest to what?
questions.explanation: This is the birthday paradox.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek philosopher posed the paradox of Achilles and the tortoise?
questions.explanation: Zeno argued that motion could not occur, since it needs infinitely many steps.

questions.question: Acrophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Acrophobia is an extreme fear of heights.

questions.question: Hydrophobia, as a phobia, is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: The word means fear of water. Historically the term was also used for a symptom of rabies.

questions.question: What is the fear of clowns called?
questions.explanation: Coulrophobia is the fear of clowns. Pediophobia is a fear of dolls.

questions.question: Nyctophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Nyctophobia is a persistent fear of night or darkness.

questions.question: Who published the general theory of relativity?
questions.explanation: Einstein presented the general theory of relativity in 1915.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: The newton (N) is the force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 m/s².

questions.question: Which law states that every action has an equal and opposite reaction?
questions.explanation: That is Newton's third law of motion.

questions.question: What name is given to the change in a wave's observed frequency when its source moves relative to the observer?
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect explains why an approaching siren sounds higher-pitched than a receding one.

questions.question: What is a photon?
questions.explanation: Light behaves as both wave and particle.

questions.question: What does Heisenberg's uncertainty principle say?
choices: Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
questions.explanation: The more precisely one is known, the less precisely the other can be.

questions.question: Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called what?
questions.explanation: Each proton is two up quarks and one down quark.

questions.question: According to special relativity, what is the maximum speed at which information can travel?
questions.explanation: Nothing with mass can reach it.

questions.question: In general relativity, what is gravity understood as?
questions.explanation: Mass tells spacetime how to curve; spacetime tells mass how to move.

questions.question: Which scientist proposed that black holes slowly emit radiation and can evaporate?
questions.explanation: This is called Hawking radiation.

questions.question: Which planet has the shortest year, orbiting the Sun in about 88 Earth days?
questions.explanation: Mercury is closest to the Sun and moves fastest, completing an orbit in about 88 days.

questions.question: What is the Great Red Spot on Jupiter?
questions.explanation: It is an enormous long-lived storm, large enough to swallow Earth.

questions.question: What is a substance called that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up?
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction and is regenerated afterwards.

questions.question: What is the process called when a solid turns directly into a gas?
questions.explanation: Dry ice turning to carbon dioxide gas is a classic example of sublimation.

questions.question: Which condition is NECESSARY for a liquid to conduct electricity well?
choices: Mobile charged particles such as ions
questions.explanation: Current needs charge carriers that can move; dissolved ions provide them. Pure water has very few ions.
questions.misconception: Many people think pure water is a good electrical conductor.

questions.question: What is 2/3 divided by 4/9?
questions.explanation: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its inverse: 2/3 × 9/4 = 18/12 = 3/2.

questions.question: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Compared with the original price, the final price is:
questions.explanation: Starting at 100: 100 × 1.2 = 120, then 120 × 0.8 = 96, which is 4% below the original.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.explanation: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes sum to 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4 and their reverses), so 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.question: A town's mean income is well above its median income. What does this most likely show?
choices: Most people earn more than the mean
A few very high earners pull the mean up
questions.explanation: A small group of very high incomes raises the mean but not the median, which marks the middle person.

questions.question: What is the greatest common divisor of 84 and 126?
questions.explanation: 126 − 84 = 42, and 42 divides 84, so the greatest common divisor is 42 (Euclid's method).

questions.question: The statement 'If it rains, the street is wet' is true, and the street is wet. What can you conclude?
choices: Nothing for certain about the rain
questions.explanation: A wet street could have other causes, so concluding it rained commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

questions.question: An argument is valid but one of its premises is false. Which description fits?
questions.explanation: Soundness needs a valid argument and true premises, so one false premise makes it unsound.

questions.question: Which number is approximately the golden ratio?
questions.explanation: The golden ratio is (1 + √5) / 2, about 1.618.

questions.question: Which metric prefix means one billionth (10⁻⁹)?
questions.explanation: Nano means 10⁻⁹. Micro is 10⁻⁶ and pico is 10⁻¹².

questions.question: What is 0.999… (the 9 repeating forever) equal to?
questions.explanation: 1/3 = 0.333… so 3 × (1/3) = 0.999… = 1. There is no number between them.

questions.question: Ophidiophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Ophidiophobia is the fear of snakes, from the Greek 'ophis', meaning serpent.

questions.question: Glossophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Glossophobia is the fear of speaking in public, one of the most common social fears.

questions.question: Triskaidekaphobia is the fear of which number?
questions.explanation: It is the fear of the number 13, which is why many buildings skip a 13th floor.

questions.question: Cynophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Cynophobia is the fear of dogs, from the Greek 'kyon'. The fear of cats is ailurophobia.

questions.question: Entomophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Entomophobia is the fear of insects in general.

questions.question: Hemophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Hemophobia is the fear of blood. It often overlaps with the fear of injury or needles.

questions.question: Agoraphobia is best described as a fear of what?
choices: Situations where escape might be hard, such as open or crowded places
questions.explanation: Agoraphobia is anxiety about places or situations where escape might be difficult. It is not only a fear of open spaces.

questions.question: Ailurophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Ailurophobia is the fear of cats.

questions.question: Mysophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Mysophobia is an extreme fear of germs, dirt or contamination.

questions.question: Trypophobia is an aversion to what?
choices: Clusters of small holes or bumps
questions.explanation: People with trypophobia feel discomfort looking at clustered holes, such as in a lotus seed pod. It is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5.

questions.question: Absolute zero is approximately what temperature in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: Absolute zero is 0 kelvin, which equals −273.15 °C.

questions.question: Which particle did J. J. Thomson discover in 1897?
questions.explanation: Thomson's cathode-ray experiments revealed the electron, the first subatomic particle found.

questions.question: Which phenomenon is mainly responsible for the blue colour of the daytime sky?
questions.explanation: Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths of sunlight much more strongly than long ones.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays sit at the high-energy, short-wavelength end of the electromagnetic spectrum.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation: The ohm (symbol Ω) is the unit of electrical resistance.

questions.question: How many joules are in one kilocalorie, approximately?
questions.explanation: One calorie is about 4.184 joules, so one kilocalorie is about 4,184 joules.
questions.misconception: Many people think a food Calorie and a calorie in physics are the same amount.

questions.question: Which element is the most abundant in the universe?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen makes up roughly three quarters of ordinary matter by mass, with helium most of the rest.

questions.question: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.explanation: At about 150 million km, light from the Sun takes roughly 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

questions.question: What is the boundary around a black hole called, beyond which nothing can escape?
questions.explanation: Past the event horizon the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

questions.question: Which astronomer formulated three laws of planetary motion in the early 1600s?
questions.explanation: Kepler's laws describe elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period–distance relationship.

questions.question: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. A person tests positive. Roughly how likely is it that they have the disease?
questions.explanation: Of 1,000 people, about 1 true case tests positive but so do about 10 healthy people, so roughly 1 in 11 positives is a true case.

questions.question: Pogonophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Pogonophobia is an irrational fear or strong dislike of beards.

questions.question: Ornithophobia is the fear of what?
questions.explanation: Ornithophobia is the fear of birds.

questions.question: The 17-syllable word 'hippopotomonstrosesquippedaliophobia' is a jocular name for the fear of what?
questions.explanation: It is a humorous coinage: a very long word for the fear of long words.

questions.question: The Chandrasekhar limit describes the maximum mass of what kind of object?
questions.explanation: Above roughly 1.4 solar masses, a white dwarf can no longer support itself against gravity.
